articles.title: Pakistan tests Fa'az missile, but reach and speed remain a mystery
articles.summary: Pakistan has announced the successful flight test of its first indigenously developed air-to-air missile, the Fa'az.
articles.body: Pakistan has announced the successful flight test of its first indigenously developed air-to-air missile, the Fa'az. The Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said the test was witnessed by senior military officers, scientists and engineers involved in its development. Equipped with a terminal guidance system, the missile is designed to engage aerial targets at longer ranges and, according to the military, will add to the Pakistan Air Force's operational flexibility. The announcement gave no details of the missile's range, speed or performance.The test comes as Pakistan expands indigenous weapons production and modernises its air force after the military confrontation with India in May 2025. Islamabad is also working with Turkey on beyond-visual-range missile technology. Pakistan's Global Industrial and Defence Solutions (GIDS) is developing the Fa'az-2, while Turkey's Tubitak Sage is working on the Gokdogan, and reports suggest the two sides could combine elements of their designs. Nothing in the available information shows that the Fa'az tested now is the FAAZ-2, so the two should be treated as separate systems for now.India's answer: the Astra familyIndia, meanwhile, is building its own family of air-to-air beyond visual range missiles, known as the Astra family of weapons. The indigenously developed Astra Mk-2 is expected to enter service either this year or in 2027, offering a range of 200 kilometres, with the Indian Air Force planning to induct as many as 700 units across its Sukhoi-30 and Tejas fleets, as per reports.Work is simultaneously underway on the more ambitious Astra Mk-3 air-to-air missile, which is also being called the Gandiva. This missile will extend the reach of the air force and navy's fighters further out to 350 kilometres using solid fuel ducted ramjet propulsion, a technology comparable to that powering Europe's Meteor missile, which is also used by the IAF's Rafale fighter aircraft. Together, the Astra series is expected to progressively replace the Russian, French and European air-to-air missiles that currently equip Indian fighter squadrons, marking a significant step toward self-reliance in one of the most technologically demanding categories of modern weaponry.This family rests on the Astra Mk-1, developed by DRDO and built by Bharat Dynamics Limited. It has a range of about 110 kilometres and is already in service on the Su-30MKI. In March 2025, a Mk-1 fired from a Tejas Mk1 prototype hit a target drone at over 100 kilometres, showing it can work with India's domestically developed light fighter. The Mk-2 missile adds range through a dual-pulse rocket motor, while the Mk-3 would take the family into the class of the longest-range air-to-air missiles in the world.

articles.title: The biggest revelations from Netflix’s Natalee Holloway doc
articles.summary: Natalee Holloway's mother, friends, and FBI agent speak out about her disappearance and the long journey to Joran van der Sloot's confession.
articles.body:
When 18-year-old Alabama high school graduate Natalee Holloway went missing during a trip to Aruba in 2005, it became a media firestorm that lasted years.

Her killer, Joran van der Sloot, didn't confess until nearly two decades later, in 2023. Her body was never found.

The Netflix docuseries "Taken: Natalee Holloway" features new interviews with Natalee's mother, Beth, her friends, FBI agents who worked on the case, and the Aruban police chief at the time.

Here are the biggest revelations from the series.

Natalee's friends weren't concerned when she drove off in a car with strangers

"When one of my friends saw Natalee in a gray Honda Civic with Joran [van der Sloot] and two Aruban guys driving, we were not really worried," said Madison Greer, one of Natalee's friends. The group met van der Sloot during a night out.

Natalee was last seen alive on May 30, 2005, leaving a bar and getting into a car with van der Sloot and brothers Deepak and Satish Kalpoe.

Greer recalled onscreen that Natalee was in high spirits at the time, "hanging out of the car, and saying like, 'Aruba!' People said 'Aruba!' back. And then, she drove off."

Natalee's friends weren't alarmed, because taxis on the island were unmarked ordinary cars, she explained.

Greer added, "There's no doubt in my mind that [Natalee] thought, '[The Kalpoe brothers] are local taxi drivers, and they're gonna take me where we want to go, and then [back] to the hotel.'"

Van der Sloot, now 39, was a 17-year-old local, at the time. He told Natalee and her friends that he was a college student from Holland, Greer said.

Natalee's mother immediately confronted van der Sloot and decided he was guilty

After Beth learned that her daughter was missing, she rushed to Aruba. Natalee's friends had shared the details about van der Sloot, and described his car. Armed with that information, Beth confronted him at his home, with his father present.

"The only thing going through my mind was, 'Find this guy, get Natalee, bring her home," Beth said.

During their confrontation, van der Sloot allegedly told Beth that he kissed Natalee on a beach, before dropping her off at her hotel, where she stumbled out of the car, hit her head, and security guards helped her inside.

Beth knew in her "gut" that van der Sloot was lying, she said. "I don't know what parts of that [account] are true, but I knew that he knew what happened to her. I decided, 'Tag, you're it,'" she recalled.

She added, "I looked at that gray Honda and I thought, 'Could Natalee be in that trunk?"

Why police took so long to arrest van der Sloot

Although van der Sloot was the primary suspect, he wasn't arrested until 10 days after Natalee's disappearance. The Kalpoe brothers were also arrested, but they were never charged in connection with Natalee's disappearance, and maintain their innocence.

Gerold Dompig, the Aruban police chief at the time, said onscreen, "We couldn't find forensic evidence, but we had so much publicity – so much pressure on Aruba."

"It was frustrating watching the news and wanting to have something happen," Greer recalled. "It made us all very angry that it was taking them this long. Why are we not arresting him?"

Before arresting van der Sloot, Aruban police first arrested two security guards from the hotel, to go along with van der Sloot's initial account that he dropped Natalee off, and security helped her inside.

"Everybody looking from the outside was only focused on Joran, but the investigation has a certain tactic that you first eliminated the noise. The security guard was noise. But to exclude them, we have to investigate," Dompig explained.

After police arrested security guards, they obtained video footage that showed that van der Sloot was lying about dropping Natalee off at her hotel.

"We needed to find that stuff which you can use to corner the suspect. We hoped that he would start to break down," said Dompig.

Van der Sloot changed his story '40 times' when police questioned him

"Normally, underaged suspects break down under interrogation. I was convinced that we were ready to try to get a confession. But Joran was very difficult to interrogate," Dompig admitted.

At the time, van der Sloot told police conflicting accounts of his night with Natalee. "He liked being the dominant one, the center of attention…he changed his story I think 40 times," said Dompig.

Then, it was revealed that van der Sloot's father, Paulus, was an attorney who was on the path to becoming a judge in Aruba.

"That complicated matters seriously, because he had more visiting rights…His father being a judge in training was a problem for us, because he could give his son certain advice," said Dompig, adding that during their investigation, they found that van der Sloot's father allegedly told him, "if there's no body, there's no crime."

The police had van der Sloot in custody for several weeks, but they had to release him on Sept. 3, 2005, due to a lack of evidence.

"The main thing that was lacking in this case was that we never found Natalee," Dompig said.

Locals felt slighted by the media coverage

Dilma Arends Geerman, an Aruban journalist, said, "Having somebody go missing is almost a slap in the face, we take care of our people."

Charles Croes, an Aruban businessman who helped Beth search for Natalee, explained that Aruba has a sense of "being kind to the visitors," because its economy depends "almost entirely" on tourism.

Geerman called it "disappointing" when the American media came and, "the impression was created that Aruba was doing nothing."

How Beth's lawyer got van der Sloot for extortion and wire fraud

In 2010, John Q. Kelly, Beth's attorney, got an email from van der Sloot, allegedly telling him, "I will take you to Natalee. In return, I want to receive $250,000."

"I thought it was complete bulls–t. I knew he had no intention of giving any truthful information whatsoever, but I told Beth there might be a play to get him trapped with extortion and fraud charge," Kelly explained, noting that American authorities had no jurisdiction in Aruba, but they could extradite van der Sloot to the United States.

When Kelly flew to Aruba and met with van der Sloot in 2010 and gave him a portion of the money, the latter told him that Natalee's body was in the cement foundation of a house that had been under construction in 2005.

"I pretended like I believed this," Kelly explained. "In theory, Joran took twenty-five grand, had a good laugh, and went about his merry way. It didn't bother me at all, because I knew how it was going to play out."

Together with FBI investigators, Kelly found that van der Sloot's story wasn't true, because the house hadn't been under construction at the time.

However, before they could take action against him for extortion and wire fraud, van der Sloot was convicted of murdering another young woman, and sentenced to prison in Peru.

Natalee's friends were angry when van der Sloot was convicted of murder in Peru

In 2012, van der Sloot pleaded guilty to the 2010 murder of 21 year old Peruvian business student Stephany Flores Ramírez. In 2012, he was sentenced to 28 years in Peruvian prison.

"I remember being angry. This could have been prevented," said Greer.

"It was devastating," said Beth. "Another young girl has lost her life, five years to the date that he murdered Natalee. I mean it was sickening. I knew he would kill again. He's just a time bomb."

Dompig was "shocked" when he heard that van der Sloot had killed Ramírez.

"Sadly, the fact that we couldn't find forensic evidence and he got away with the Natalee case made him more dangerous. I think if he was not in prison, he would kill again."

Van der Sloot alleged that he killed a rabbit

In 2023, FBI agents extradited van der Sloot to Birmingham, Alabama. Retired FBI agent Alexandra Montilla explained, "We cannot indict him on charges of murdering Natalee, but we'll get you on the extortion charges, and we'll get you in Natalee's backyard."

Montilla, who was on the plane with van der Sloot as he was flown from Peru to Alabama at the time, recalled that he was "charismatic, easy to talk to…people are drawn to him. He comes off as a very educated man."

During the flight, van der Sloot, who had married and had a daughter during his time in prison, allegedly told Montilla that he was allowed to have a bunny, but when the animal scratched his daughter, he, "grabbed the bunny rabbit and ripped his head off like it was nothing," she said.

After allegedly revealing that, van der Sloot, "carried on with other conversations," Montilla claimed.

Montilla noted, "I've dealt with a lot of criminals, and as a female, I thought, 'this is probably one of the most dangerous ones.'"

The FBI interviewer decided van der Sloot was being truthful because he'd been to Aruba

While van der Sloot was extradited to Alabama, he confessed under a polygraph to bludgeoning Natalee to death on a beach in Aruba. He claimed that he waded three yards into the ocean, and disposed of her body there.

Scott, a former FBI agent, explained that van der Sloot agreed to a plea deal to provide the information, in exchange for the government recommending to the court "that the sentence would be concurrent with the sentence he is serving in Peru."

Michael Leverock, the retired FBI agent who was van der Sloot's polygraph examiner, recalled, "The one part of the story that everyone had a problem with is that 3 yards out into the water, it just doesn't sound right. Generally, you can't just put somebody in the ocean. They're gonna wash up."

However, Leverock recalled that he had recently taken his own trip to Aruba, and he learned that the relevant area of the island has, "an offshore wind," which means, "if something happens [to a person] out there, they're not coming back in."

Beth said that listening to van der Sloot's confession was, "hard to hear, horrible to hear, but I had to hear it. The not knowing is the most torturous part."

Currently, van der Sloot is serving his sentence in Peru.

"Taken: Natalee Holloway" is now streaming on Netflix.

articles.title: Peaky Blinders helped put Birmingham on the global tourism map; a new study estimates film and TV links could bring £66.97 million to the West Midlands
articles.summary: The popularity of Peaky Blinders has helped introduce Birmingham and the wider West Midlands to audiences around the world, turning filming locations into
articles.body: The popularity of Peaky Blinders has helped introduce Birmingham and the wider West Midlands to audiences around the world, turning filming locations into attractions for fans of the drama. A new study by creative industries consultancy OlsbergSPI estimates that connections to film and television could generate £66.97 million in visitor spending across the region. The research suggests that screen productions can influence travel decisions, encourage additional visits and bring financial benefits to local attractions, accommodation providers and other tourism businesses.Peaky Blinders helped put Birmingham on the global tourism mapThe BBC drama Peaky Blinders, which ran from 2013 to 2022, has become one of the most recognisable television productions associated with Birmingham. Created by Birmingham-born writer Steven Knight and starring Cillian Murphy as Tommy Shelby, the series follows a fictional criminal gang operating in the city during the period of industrial change following the First World War.Although the story is rooted in Birmingham, the programme has attracted viewers from across the world, particularly in the United States. Its popularity has also brought attention to locations across the West Midlands, including the Black Country Living Museum in Dudley, where some of the show's most recognisable scenes were filmed.According to BirminghamWorld, the series has played an important role in raising the city's international profile. Birmingham has also hosted world premieres for successive seasons, while the 2018 Peaky Blinders Festival brought together hundreds of actors from the production and featured a performance by Liam Gallagher.The programme's influence has extended beyond television. A dance production based on the series was created by Rambert, adding another cultural attraction connected to the story.What the new study found about screen tourismThe potential economic contribution of film and television tourism has now been examined through a pilot study conducted by OlsbergSPI in partnership with the Black Country Living Museum.The research involved a virtual survey of more than 5,000 national and international visitors who had visited the museum since the first release of Peaky Blinders in 2013. The survey was distributed through the attraction's mailing lists and social media channels to understand what encouraged people to visit and how much screen-related interest contributed to their spending.The findings showed that around 4% of museum visitors came mainly because of Peaky Blinders. While this represented a relatively small share of overall attendance, the group had a notable economic impact. Visitors motivated by the programme spent, on average, between 20% and 30% more than those who visited for other reasons.The findings suggest that screen tourism does not necessarily depend on attracting enormous numbers of additional visitors. People travelling specifically because of a film or television production may spend more during their visit, creating additional value for the attraction and the surrounding tourism economy.How could film and television generate £66.97 millionThe study also examined the wider impact of screen productions across the West Midlands rather than focusing exclusively on the museum.OlsbergSPI found that 6% of survey respondents would not have visited the region if it had no connections to film and television. The consultancy used this additional visitor interest to estimate the potential contribution of screen tourism to the area's economy.According to its findings, the West Midlands recorded 1.99 million inbound visits in 2024, based on figures from VisitBritain. Assuming that the survey's 6% proportion applied to all those visits, the consultancy estimated that film and television connections could support approximately 126,600 inbound visits. Those visits could generate an estimated £66.97 million in visitor expenditure.The figure represents projected spending associated with screen tourism rather than money already received by regional businesses. It is based on the assumption that the survey findings reflect the motivations of the wider population of inbound visitors.The Screen Tourism pamphlet published by Olsberg•SPI also highlights the importance of measuring whether screen productions genuinely encourage additional travel. Its research found that around 3% of international Black Country Living Museum visitors were motivated purely by film and television to visit the UK, while approximately 2% were specifically motivated by Peaky Blinders.Screen tourism can benefit more than filming locationsThe financial impact of screen tourism can extend well beyond the attractions featured on television. Visitors travelling to experience places connected to their favourite productions may also spend money on accommodation, restaurants, transport, entry tickets and other local experiences.OlsbergSPI explains that this wider spending can support employment and encourage further investment in destinations. Film and television productions can also introduce regional heritage, architecture and cultural attractions to international audiences who might otherwise have little reason to visit.For the West Midlands, this creates an opportunity to connect its industrial history and existing visitor attractions with the international popularity of television and film.The Black Country Living Museum has already developed experiences around this interest. The attraction regularly hosts Peaky Blinders Nights, allowing visitors to dress in period-inspired clothing and take part in themed activities.Could Birmingham develop a permanent Peaky Blinders attractionThe possibility of creating a dedicated attraction connected to the series has also been discussed in Birmingham.In February 2023, BirminghamWorld reported that tourism officials were responding to speculation about a possible Peaky Blinders theme park. Although the reports of a theme park had not been confirmed, the West Midlands Growth Company indicated that a more permanent visitor experience was worth exploring.Its chief executive, Neil Rami, said the organisation had launched a feasibility study to investigate whether a new attraction or experience celebrating the series could be viable.Birmingham City Council leader Ian Ward also highlighted the city's importance to the programme, noting that Birmingham and the Black Country had been presented to millions of viewers in Britain and internationally.He also pointed to the region's growing appeal as a filming destination, with major productions involving filmmakers such as Steven Spielberg and Tom Cruise having used the city.You use AI every day. articles.body: The death toll from the October 10 attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh has risen to 14 after a second Indian national injured in the strike died in hospital, the Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia said on Wednesday.The victim, whose identity has not been disclosed, had been critically injured and was being treated in an intensive care unit (ICU). The toll rose to 13 after the first injured Indian national died and has now reached 14.Saudi Arabia blamed Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels for the attack, although the group did not officially claim responsibility. The strike was part of a wider escalation in attacks on Saudi infrastructure amid the renewed conflict in Yemen.The latest death also comes amid a rising toll among Indians caught up in the wider West Asia conflict. articles.title: ‘Habibi, call me Senator’: First Muslim US Senator Abdul El-Sayed mocks Donald Trump, JD Vance in victory speech
articles.summary: Democrat candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Wednesday took a swipe at US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance after defeating Republican Mike
articles.body: Democrat candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Wednesday took a swipe at US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance after defeating Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's Senate race, using his victory speech to highlight the irony of Vance having to formally swear him into office.Addressing Vance, El-Sayed said, “Habibi, there is this delicious irony in the fact that you’re constitutionally obligated to swear me in, in January.”He also directed a pointed message at Trump, who had repeatedly criticised him during the campaign and questioned his loyalty to the United States.“I know you struggle with my name, so after JD swears me in, you can just go on and call me Senator,” El-Sayed said.El-Sayed's victory makes him the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. He defeated Rogers, a former congressman and FBI agent who had Trump's backing, in a closely watched contest for Michigan's open Senate seat.El-Sayed also took aim at Rogers during his victory speech, telling supporters, “You chose hate, and Michigan chose hope.”El-Sayed's campaign and attacks from TrumpThe son of Egyptian immigrants, El-Sayed is a former public health official who had never held elected office before winning the Senate race. His victory followed a difficult political journey, eight years after he suffered a double-digit defeat in Michigan's Democratic gubernatorial primary.His campaign was built around a progressive platform that included universal healthcare, removing outside money from elections and criticism of Israel. He received support from progressive leaders, including Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.The campaign was marked by repeated attacks from Trump and other Republicans, who sought to link El-Sayed to terrorist organisations despite no evidence of such ties. They also questioned his loyalty to the US.El-Sayed's criticism of Israel became a major point of contention, including during a bruising Democratic primary against Representative Haley Stevens. The primary drew nearly $60 million in outside spending, with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) spending nearly $30 million opposing him, its largest investment in a single race.Stevens, who lost the primary, endorsed Rogers on November 1, saying El-Sayed had not done enough to address her and the Jewish community's concerns.El-Sayed also faced criticism over remarks following an attack on a Michigan synagogue earlier this year. He later apologised, saying he was “sorry” to “anyone who feels like my comments might have been hurtful”.Democratic gains reshape Senate politicsEl-Sayed's win came as Democrats secured control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, according to Reuters. His victory was among several gains for the party in states that have traditionally favoured Republicans.The Michigan contest became a major focus in the battle for Senate control after two-term Democratic Senator Gary Peters decided not to seek re-election.Republicans had cleared the field for Rogers, who narrowly lost a Senate race to then-Representative Elissa Slotkin in 2024.However, his campaign faced challenges over his support for Trump as voters expressed concerns about rising prices linked to the war with Iran and the economic impact of the president's tariffs.Rogers, who had previously criticised Trump, had aligned himself more closely with the president in recent years.He had also voiced concern about the war with Iran, writing on social media in September, “The war with Iran needs to end, and end quickly.”El-Sayed's victory is expected to strengthen the progressive wing of the Democratic Party ahead of the 2028 presidential election.His campaign demonstrated the electoral reach of a platform centred on policies such as Medicare for All, which would replace the existing mix of private and public health insurance with a government-run, single-payer system.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Georgia man left a hospital ER barefoot and was killed crossing the road; his wife and estate won a $7.5 million jury verdict, but an appeals court upheld its reversal because medical causation was not proved
articles.summary: Life is very unpredictable; situations may change within a moment and lead to sudden surprises, just like what happened to a Georgia man.
articles.body: Life is very unpredictable; situations may change within a moment and lead to sudden surprises, just like what happened to a Georgia man. Gerber's trip to the emergency room was supposed to help him but ended in tragedy that would later become the subject of a lengthy legal fight. Gerber spent only about an hour at a Georgia hospital before walking out barefoot and being struck by a vehicle as he tried to cross the road. His wife, Hopkins, and his estate later sued the medical team, claiming the hospital didn’t properly assess and care for him. A jury awarded them $7.5 million in damages initially. But now the Court of Appeals of Georgia has upheld the overturning of that verdict, saying the family could not prove the alleged medical negligence caused his death.What went on in the hospital?The Court of Appeals of Georgia says it all began when Gerber showed up at his wife’s home drunk and in an agitated state. Hopkins called emergency services after he saw blood in his stool. Paramedics arrived to find him confused, unsteady and struggling to communicate. He was unable to tell what year it was and required help to walk.Gerber was transported to Liberty Regional Medical Center, where hospital staff was informed of his condition. He was sent to a shower room because his clothes were dirty. His medical records also showed a blood pressure reading of 188/118, and he had reported feeling nauseous, vomiting and suffering from diarrhea in the weeks prior.Even with these symptoms the hospital did not admit him for further treatment. The court’s account said the attending physician wrote in the notes that Gerber was alert and wanted to leave, and determined there was no medical reason to keep him there.He left without shoes and was hit by a vehicleBefore leaving Gerber asked hospital staff to call Hopkins to pick him up. She refused, saying there was a temporary protective order in place, but had voiced concern about his health. Employees at the hospital tried to flag down a cab and called the Sheriff’s Department, but were unable to get him a ride.About 70 minutes later Gerber left the emergency department in his soiled clothes, minus his shoes. He was trying to cross the road outside the hospital when he was hit by an oncoming vehicle. The crash was fatal.His wife and estate later sued the hospital authority, the attending physician and a nurse, saying the medical team didn’t properly care for him and didn’t take reasonable steps to protect him.Jury awards $7.5MAt first the case went in the family’s favor. The jury apportioned a significant percentage of the damages to the medical professionals and hospital, finding the physician 40% at fault, the nurse and hospital also 40%, and Gerber 20%.The final award was $7.5 million. But the defendants challenged the verdict, saying the family had failed to show sufficient evidence linking the alleged medical failures with the fatal accident.In the end, the trial court agreed and reversed the jury’s verdict. Hopkins and the estate appealed to the Court of Appeals of Georgia.Why appeals court rejected awardThe key question was not whether Gerber received better medical care, but whether that failure could be shown to have caused his death.The family's medical expert testified that Gerber needed a more extensive exam, proper treatment and a clearer explanation of the risks of leaving the hospital. But the expert could not say what his state of mind was when he walked out, or that a different medical evaluation would have kept him in.In a November 3, 2026 ruling, the Court of Appeals of Georgia found that the evidence did not establish the necessary nexus between the alleged negligence and the fatal collision. It also found that the accident was an intervening event which could not be seen as a foreseeable consequence of the alleged failure of the hospital to treat him.The appeals court thus affirmed the overturning of the $7.5 million jury award.Images Courtesy: istockYou use AI every day. articles.title: SC issues notice to Centre, poll body on blanket immunity to CEC
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Wednesday sought a response from the Centre and the Election Commission over a plea challenging immunity to Chief Election
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Wednesday sought a response from the Centre and the Election Commission over a plea challenging immunity to Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners from any legal action for any decision taken in the course of their duties.A bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohanna issued notice to the poll body and Centre on a petition filed by activist and lawyer Arun Kumar Agarwal.According to Bar and Bench, the plea challenges the constitutional validity of Section 16 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023."Despite the absence of such blanket immunity, the Election Commission of India has successfully conducted elections over several decades. This shows that the Commission can function effectively without granting its members blanket immunity from legal proceedings," the plea said."The objective of protecting Election Commissioners from vexatious proceedings can be achieved through less restrictive measures, such as safeguards against frivolous complaints and prior judicial scrutiny. Granting blanket immunity is therefore excessive and goes beyond what is necessary to protect the independence of the Election Commission," it added."The said section takes away every civil and criminal remedy against the CEC and ECs for their acts. A voter whose name is wrongly deleted from the electoral roll, a candidate prejudiced by a mala fide act, and any citizen aggrieved by corruption in the functioning of the Commission are left without a remedy," it further said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Former police federation treasurer jailed for 2 years and 3 months after making more than 100 fraudulent claims to fund family holidays, alcohol and entertainment
articles.summary: A former police officer and West Mercia Police Federation treasurer has been jailed for using colleagues’ funds to pay for family holidays, alcohol, meals
articles.body: A former police officer and West Mercia Police Federation treasurer has been jailed for using colleagues’ funds to pay for family holidays, alcohol, meals and entertainment. Jamie Harrison, 55, from Droitwich, Worcestershire, made more than 100 fraudulent expense claims while serving as the federation’s secretary and treasurer between 2010 and 2018. According to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), he repeatedly used petty cash under his control for personal spending, keeping claims below £100 to avoid scrutiny. The fraud amounted to approximately £13,500. Harrison was convicted of 15 counts of fraud by abuse of position and sentenced to two years and three months in prison.How did the former police federation treasurer misuse officers' fundsHarrison served as secretary and treasurer of West Mercia Police Federation (WMPF) between 2010 and 2018. His responsibilities included safeguarding the financial interests of fellow police officers. However, he repeatedly used the federation’s petty cash, which was under his sole control, to pay for personal expenses.According to the CPS, Harrison deliberately kept his claims below £100 to avoid scrutiny. The fraudulent claims covered food, alcohol and entertainment, with the total value of the fraud estimated at approximately £13,500. He was convicted of 15 counts of fraud by abuse of position at Hereford Crown Court.Harrison also used his attendance at National Police Memorial Days as an opportunity to take his wife and children on family holidays at the federation’s expense. The occasions were organised to honour police officers who had lost their lives in the line of duty.According to the CPS, the family stayed in four- and five-star hotels in York, Cardiff, Edinburgh and London. Harrison claimed the costs of accommodation, meals and day trips from funds contributed by fellow officers. The expenses were submitted despite being personal family holiday costs.What did the investigation reveal about Harrison's false timesheetsThe investigation also found that Harrison received salary payments for days when he was not at work. He submitted timesheets falsely recording full working days, while text messages showed that he had taken time off to watch rugby abroad, including trips to Italy and Ireland.The messages also showed that he had spent time working on his allotment during periods recorded as full working days. The CPS said these false timesheets formed part of the fraudulent activity uncovered during the investigation.What prison sentence did Harrison receive for abusing his positionHarrison was convicted of 15 counts of fraud by abuse of position following a five-week trial at Hereford Crown Court. The BBC reported that he was cleared of one additional count of fraud, while the jury failed to reach a verdict on the final count.On 25 March 2026, Harrison was sentenced at Worcester Crown Court to two years and three months in prison for each charge, with the sentences to run concurrently, according to the CPS. He had resigned from West Mercia Police in February 2022.Victoria Norman of the Crown Prosecution Service said Harrison had exploited his position and control over the federation’s finances for personal gain. She said: "Harrison displayed an extremely cavalier attitude to being caught, dipping into petty cash at will, claiming expenses far beyond what was reasonable and falsifying timesheets."Norman added that his conduct had betrayed the colleagues whose subscriptions funded the Police Federation. She said the CPS was determined to bring public servants who committed fraud and abused positions of trust to justice.Why was Harrison suspended from his Police Federation roleWest Mercia Police said concerns about Harrison were first raised with the national Police Federation in June 2018. Auditors were subsequently commissioned to review the federation’s financial accounts before Harrison was suspended from his role.Detective Superintendent Tony Garner of West Mercia Police described Harrison’s actions as a betrayal of trust. He said: "Jamie Harrison chose to act for himself." Garner added that Harrison's actions amounted to criminal behaviour and that the investigation had been conducted "without fear or favour".You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Donald Trump loses US Congress; Netanyahu faces deadlock at home: What happens to Iran war now?
articles.summary: Two elections, two political setbacks and one unresolved war.
articles.body: Two elections, two political setbacks and one unresolved war. US President Donald Trump has lost control of Congress after voters handed Democrats a sweeping victory in US midterms, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is struggling to secure a parliamentary majority following Israel's October 27 elections. Both leaders, who joined forces in the war against Iran, now face growing pressure at home even as the conflict they launched remains unresolved.Months after the killing of Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, the war has neither delivered a decisive outcome nor brought Washington and Tehran closer to a lasting settlement. With Trump's Republicans losing both chambers of Congress and Netanyahu's bloc falling short of a majority in the Knesset, the political landscape has changed for both leaders.The timing is significant. US strikes on Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz came just hours before Americans voted, amid continuing exchanges of proposals between Washington and Tehran. They also followed reports that Netanyahu had pressed Trump to consider another round of military action.With both leaders facing pressure at home, where does the Trump-Bibi partnership go from here? Will the political setbacks push them towards a deal with Iran, or make them more inclined to take a harder line?Trump's midterm setback: Democrats take control of CongressThe November 3 midterm elections delivered a major blow to Trump, with Democrats winning control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. The Associated Press reported that Democrats flipped at least seven Senate seats, including in Kansas, Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina. They also gained more than two dozen House districts, including in areas that had backed Trump by double-digit margins in 2024.Trump brushed aside suggestions that the result was a personal setback, pointing out that he was not on the ballot. “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” he said.He later congratulated Democrats but maintained that the result was not a referendum on him. “The Democrats did a good job. They fought hard,” he told Fox News. “I don’t view it as a hit on me,” he added, claiming that the country had seen “the greatest two years in the history of the presidency”.The Senate results included a series of Democratic victories in traditionally Republican states. James Talarico defeated Ken Paxton in Texas, becoming the first Democrat to win a Senate election in the state since 1988. Annie Andrews defeated Darline Graham in South Carolina, while Adam Hamilton unseated incumbent Roger Marshall in Kansas, ending a 94-year gap since the state last elected a Democrat to the Senate.Democrat Josh Turek defeated Republican Ashley Hinson in Iowa, former Ohio senator Sherrod Brown beat incumbent Jon Husted, and former North Carolina governor Roy Cooper won the open Senate seat against Michael Whatley. Democrats also held on to seats in Georgia, where Jon Ossoff won re-election, and New Hampshire, where Chris Pappas defeated former senator John Sununu.Talarico celebrated his Texas victory by telling supporters: “We just took back Texas.” He added: “We are tired of being told to hate each other. We didn’t win this race by alienating our neighbors or shaming our neighbors.”The gubernatorial results also brought gains for Democrats. Keisha Lance Bottoms won in Georgia, becoming the first Black woman elected governor in the US. Amy Acton defeated Trump-backed Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio, Rob Sand won in Iowa and Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican incumbent Greg Abbott in Texas, becoming the state’s first Latina governor. Democrats also won Nevada, where Aaron Ford defeated incumbent Joe Lombardo.There were notable results for Indian-American candidates as well. Democrat Suhas Subramanyam retained his Virginia House seat, while Pia Dandiya won Florida’s 22nd Congressional District. Maryland lieutenant governor Aruna Miller also won another term alongside governor Wes Moore.The new Congress will take office in January. Democrats will have greater powers to scrutinise the administration, hold hearings, investigate Trump's actions and block or delay presidential nominees. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries is also poised to become the first Black speaker of the House, subject to a vote by lawmakers.The change could complicate Trump's domestic agenda and increase scrutiny of the Iran war. However, a Democratic-controlled Congress cannot automatically end the conflict or take military command away from the president. Trump remains commander-in-chief, while Congress can use its oversight and funding powers to exert pressure.JNU professor Rajan Kumar told TOI that the new Congress could act as a check on Trump's approach towards Iran. “He'll be balanced by the new Congress where the Democrats would be dominant. So that will play some role,” he said, adding that the president would face challenges in securing congressional approval for funding a prolonged war.Trump has warned that he would veto legislation he considers unacceptable. “They'll send over things that are insane, and I'll veto them,” he said. He also left open the possibility of working with Democrats, suggesting that after a few months of vetoes, lawmakers would ask how to get things done and “we'll work together”.Did the Iran war cost Trump at the ballot box?The election results suggest that the Iran war was one part of wider voter dissatisfaction with the administration, rather than the only reason Republicans lost control of Congress.Reuters reported that nearly nine in 10 voters identified the cost of living as a crucial or major factor in their vote, according to exit polls. Three-quarters were angry or dissatisfied with the direction of the country, while nearly two-thirds blamed Trump for high prices.The AP Voter Poll, which surveyed about 80,000 voters across the country, found that about six in 10 disapproved of Trump's handling of the presidency. Around seven in 10 said Congress was not doing enough to check presidential power.The Iran conflict also featured in voters' concerns. The AP poll found that about six in 10 voters considered the US decision to take military action against Iran the wrong one, while around a third said the war was a crucial factor in their vote.Trump acknowledged that Iran played a part in the Republican losses, but did not indicate that he regretted the military campaign.“I think a part of it was Iran, but at the same time people understood the importance of what I've done with Iran,” he told Fox News.He also defended the decision to use force, saying: “I did the right thing. I would have done it again.”Kumar told TOI that the Iran conflict had added to the wider dissatisfaction with the Trump administration, particularly because it had failed to deliver a decisive outcome.“On the issue of Iran, first, he could not achieve any military or political breakthrough. The United States got caught in a quagmire kind of situation where it's a deadlock and he can neither win nor withdraw,” he said.Kumar also pointed to the economic consequences of the conflict, saying the rise in diesel and fuel prices had contributed to the pressure on American households. He said domestic inflation remained a major concern, even though the US economy itself was not doing badly.He added that Trump had promised not to intervene in international conflicts but had acted contrary to that commitment in Venezuela and Iran, among other places.Strikes near Hormuz: Is Trump preparing for another round?Even as election results came in, the military situation remained unsettled.The Associated Press reported that the US carried out limited strikes on Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz on November 2, hours before Americans voted. Iranian state media reported explosions on Qeshm and Hengam islands and near Bandar Abbas.A US official told the AP that the strikes targeted Iranian forces using surface-to-air missiles against US assets in the strait. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment publicly.Reuters reported that US officials described the strikes as defensive and said they did not amount to a return to major combat operations. Trump later described the action as a “minor attack” and said it “wasn’t war”.He also explained the target of the operation, saying: “They built an anti-aircraft facility. It took them about two months. We watched it get built. As soon as it was completed, we hit it last night.”The strikes came amid uncertainty over whether Trump would order a fresh campaign after the midterms. The administration has maintained a naval blockade around Iranian ports, while thousands of US troops remain in the region. The AP has also reported that another aircraft carrier and additional troops are heading towards the Middle East.Diplomatic contacts have continued alongside the military build-up.Reuters reported on November 3, citing a senior Iranian official, that Washington and Tehran remained far from reaching an agreement despite intensified efforts by mediators. Qatari officials have been involved in passing proposals between the two sides.Iran has said it is prepared to discuss its nuclear programme but wants the US to lift its naval blockade and ease sanctions on its oil sales. Tehran has also sought a ceasefire that includes Lebanon. It has maintained that the Strait of Hormuz cannot be fully reopened without its conditions being addressed.Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf said Washington had the responsibility to prevent a return to war. “The ball is now in America’s court to prevent war,” he said. He warned that Iran's armed forces remained on high defensive readiness and that any further US “strategic miscalculation” would face a response on a “new battlefield”.Qalibaf later posted: “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message.” He warned that if the US government betrayed public will, it would learn that Iran’s “NO comes with a Nightmare”.The gap between the two sides remains wide. Washington wants a settlement addressing Iran’s actions in the strait and its nuclear programme, while Tehran is seeking relief from the blockade and sanctions before broader negotiations.Vice-President JD Vance has expressed optimism about a negotiated settlement. “Both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement,” he said.Netanyahu's Israel election setback: 53 seats, but no majorityThe October 27 election in Israel has left Netanyahu with a difficult task: finding a path to a parliamentary majority.The final results gave the bloc aligned with Netanyahu 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset. The opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot won 48, while Arab-led parties secured 19 seats, according to the final tally reported by The Times of Israel.Neither of the two main blocs has the 61 seats required to form a government. Netanyahu’s Likud remained the single largest party with 27 seats, while Eisenkot’s Yashar won 21. The 19 seats secured by Arab-led parties marked a record for them in an Israeli election.The Congressional Research Service, in its October 30 report on the election and government formation, noted that both major blocs had fallen short of a majority and highlighted the potential role of Arab-led parties in determining who could form the next government.Netanyahu could try to bring more parties into his existing alliance or seek a broader arrangement. The opposition is attempting to build an alternative around Eisenkot but faces divisions over whether and how to work with Arab-led parties.Netanyahu has not automatically lost office. He remains prime minister while the government formation process moves ahead. Israeli President Isaac Herzog is expected to consult political parties before asking a candidate to form a coalition. Negotiations could be difficult, particularly because the opposition does not have a clear route to 61 seats either.Election fraud allegations complicate Netanyahu's coalition battleThe election has also been followed by allegations of irregularities, with Netanyahu’s Likud questioning aspects of the result and raising claims involving Arab-led parties.“The elections in the State of Israel were stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the elimination of the Jewish state through serious criminal offences of bribery, threats, violence, forgeries, and the use of prohibited software to mobilize voters,” Netanyahu said after election setback.The opposition has rejected the allegations. Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of an “orchestrated and organised campaign to delegitimise the results”. He also described him as a “caretaker prime minister, without a mandate and without public confidence”.Netanyahu was also rebuked by President Isaac Herzog for “tarnishing an entire community”.The Jerusalem Post reported that the Israeli election commission rejected efforts to delay certification of the results over claims of interference. Israeli authorities have examined the allegations, but they have not established evidence of systematic fraud that would alter the final tally.The dispute matters because the next stage will test whether parties that have spent years divided over Netanyahu can agree on an alternative. Some opposition leaders have backed Eisenkot, but cooperation with Arab-led parties remains contentious. Avigdor Lieberman, among others, has ruled out such a partnership.The possibility of another election cannot be ruled out if coalition talks fail. For now, however, Netanyahu has time to negotiate and remains in office.Did Netanyahu push Trump to resume strikes on Iran after the midterms?The Israeli election has also raised questions about whether Netanyahu could seek a renewed military campaign against Iran as he tries to navigate the political deadlock.The Associated Press reported on November 2, citing two regional officials and another person familiar with the matter, that Netanyahu had pressed Trump to launch another wave of strikes after the US midterm elections. One of the officials said Netanyahu was working with senior US administration figures to persuade Trump to approve a quick but extensive air campaign.The AP report also said Trump had not committed to military action during a weekend call with Netanyahu. The White House did not directly respond to questions about the discussion, while the Israeli government did not immediately comment.The report does not establish that Netanyahu’s political position was the reason for seeking further strikes. The possibility that renewed conflict could help him build an emergency government has been raised in reporting and political discussion, but remains an interpretation, not an established motive.There is also a regional cost to escalation. The AP cited concerns among US allies in the Middle East that fresh attacks could destabilise the region further, draw in Iran-aligned groups and put shipping routes under greater pressure.For Netanyahu, a renewed confrontation could reinforce the security argument central to his politics. But it could also expose Israel to further retaliation and make the formation of a stable government more difficult.Kumar told TOI that Netanyahu's approach had also contributed to Trump's political difficulties.“He got kind of persuaded by Netanyahu's dream, where he thought that he can fix the Iran issue forever. But in the process, he got the US involved,” he said.Kumar added that Trump's support for Netanyahu during the Israeli election had generated resentment among some opposition supporters. “Instead of pursuing a policy of neutrality, in Israel also he played a politics where he endorsed the candidacy of Netanyahu,” he said.Two political setbacks, one Iran war: What happens next?The political consequences of the two elections are different, but they could affect the same conflict.Trump will have to deal with a Congress controlled by Democrats from January, while Netanyahu needs to find a way to form a government. Both have reasons to show that they remain in control of events, but neither has a free hand.For Trump, the election result makes it harder to sustain a war without facing questions from Congress and voters. Democrats can investigate the administration’s decisions, demand information on the cost and objectives of the campaign and use hearings to keep the issue in the public eye. They cannot, simply by winning the midterms, order the president to end military operations.For Netanyahu, the immediate challenge is domestic. His bloc has 53 seats, and the opposition is trying to organise around Eisenkot. A broader security crisis could change the political debate, but it would also carry risks for Israel and its regional relationships. There is no certainty that another round of strikes would help Netanyahu secure a majority.Kumar said the direction of the conflict would depend partly on how Israeli politics unfolded in the coming weeks. He also cautioned that Trump could still pursue a coercive approach towards Iran, even as the new Congress seeks to limit his options.“Trump being Trump is very unpredictable,” Kumar told TOI. “His policy has backfired domestically as well as in terms of foreign policy.”The president’s own statements suggest that Trump is still weighing both military and diplomatic options. His decision to describe the latest strikes as limited, while continuing to defend the wider campaign, leaves room for further action as well as negotiations.The immediate test will be whether the US and Iran can turn the proposals being exchanged through Qatar into an agreement addressing the blockade, shipping through Hormuz and the wider conflict. If they fail, military pressure could rise again.For Netanyahu, the next few weeks will be dominated by coalition arithmetic. For Trump, they will be about what the war has achieved, what it is costing and how much political support remains for continuing it.The elections have not ended the Iran war. They have, however, made it harder for both leaders to ignore the domestic consequences of what happens next.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Khamenei is dead, long live the Ayatollah! How Trump's Iran war triggered 'regime change' at home
articles.summary: Donald Trump appeared to have discovered a formula for changing regimes.
articles.body: Donald Trump appeared to have discovered a formula for changing regimes. In January, US forces captured Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro, leaving Washington with extraordinary leverage over Caracas and its vast oil reserves. The message from Trump: The US is willing to use force and expects results.Iran seemed next in line. On February 28, the US and Israel launched their military operation against the Islamic Republic, killing Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Trump asked Iranians to "take over your government", describing it as their "only chance for generations".But Tehran did not oblige. The Islamic Republic survived, Khamenei's son Mojtaba was named his successor, and the country's security establishment emerged with even greater influence. The promised revolution did not arrive. Instead, the old order has adapted, hardened and is carrying on.The more consequential political upheaval, however, has now come thousands of miles away. In the midterm elections, Democrats have captured both the House of Representatives and the Senate, delivering a sweeping rebuke to Trump. The president who wanted to change the political order in Tehran has found the "regime changing" in his own United States.The illusionTrump's first miscalculation was to treat the Islamic Republic as a one-man system. The assumption behind leadership decapitation is that removing the person at the top can destabilise the entire structure beneath him. But Iran's political order is not held together by the supreme leader alone. It rests on a network of clerical institutions, security agencies, political patrons and, crucially, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).The warning signs were there. Danny Citrinowicz of the Atlantic Council told Reuters: "The Iranian system is bigger than one man. Removing Khamenei could harden the regime rather than weaken it." Ali Hashem, a research affiliate at Royal Holloway, University of London, made the point even more directly: "Iran was built to survive the loss of a leader."That is precisely what happened. Khamenei's killing did not produce the mass defections or immediate popular uprising that could have turned a military operation into regime collapse. Instead, the system moved towards institutional survival. The IRGC and other security institutions gained greater influence as Iran entered a wartime leadership transition. The result was not the collapse of the Islamic Republic but its hardening into a more security-dominated state.The decapitation strategy removed the regime's most powerful individual, but not the institutions capable of reproducing its power. The external attack also gave competing centres of authority a common reason to close ranks.There was an economic miscalculation too. After Maduro's capture, Washington appeared to have gained considerable leverage over Venezuela's oil sector. The implicit hope was that Venezuelan production could provide a buffer if the Iran confrontation disrupted supplies from the Gulf. But oil is not interchangeable simply because it comes from another country.Much of Venezuela's oil is extra-heavy crude, requiring specialised processing and blending. Its ageing infrastructure and limited production capacity also make a rapid increase in output difficult. More importantly, Venezuelan crude cannot simply replace the lighter and medium grades disrupted by the closure or restriction of flows through the Strait of Hormuz."Venezuela cannot replace that, also partly because it is a different grade, namely, heavy, sour crude," Frederic Schneider of the Middle East Council on Global Affairs told Al Jazeera.The US gained leverage over Venezuelan barrels, but it has not been able to conjure an immediate substitute for Gulf supplies.The real battlefield in USFor American voters, the consequences of the Iran war were not measured in military briefings or geopolitical maps. They were measured at petrol stations and supermarket checkouts.The national average price of gasoline reached around $4.17 a gallon on November 2, the day before the midterms, according to figures cited by The Washington Post. That was 37 cents above the previous election day record set in 2022. Another report put the average at $4.22 on October 29, compared with about $3.03 a year earlier.Trump did little to soften the political impact. At a campaign stop in North Carolina in September, he described higher fuel prices as "a very inexpensive price to pay for what we've done". At a rally in Georgia in October, he was even more blunt: "I don't give a damn. I'm going to say it. We're making a freaking fortune."ALSO READ | Iran war, inflation or Trump fatigue: What drove Democrats' midterm surge?These remarks were meant to underline the gains Trump believed US was making from higher oil prices. But they also exposed the gap between the administration's economic argument and the experience of households paying more to fill their tanks. For voters, the distinction between profits for the oil industry and rising household expenses offered little comfort.The squeeze extended beyond fuel. Inflation remained stubborn, consumer confidence was near historic lows and voters were increasingly concerned about the cost of everyday essentials. The Iran conflict added to an already difficult economic picture, making it harder for the White House to sell its foreign-policy ambitions as evidence of national strength.The financial cost of the war added another layer to the argument. An Associated Press report put the estimated cost to American taxpayers at $47.1 billion as of October 16. Around $29 billion was attributed to replacing munitions, $11.9 billion to operations and $6 billion to equipment losses. The estimate did not include damage to US bases from Iranian attacks.America first or America at war?The political damage was not confined to voters worried about prices. The Iran escalation also threatened to fracture Trump's own coalition. His appeal in 2016, and again in 2024, rested partly on his promise to end America's endless wars and put domestic interests ahead of foreign entanglements.The confrontation with Iran put that promise under strain. It gave progressives and independent voters another reason to oppose the administration, while creating unease among anti-interventionist conservatives who had backed Trump's rejection of the Washington foreign-policy establishment. For them, the escalation looked less like America First and more like a return to the neoconservative playbook.The wider geopolitical consequences were also far from the picture of unchallenged American dominance. China remained a major buyer of Iranian oil, much of it transported through shadow-fleet networks designed to evade sanctions. Beijing has helped Tehran sustain oil revenues, although it has stopped short of a formal defence commitment. Russia, meanwhile, has maintained its strategic relationship with Iran.The conflict may have increased pressure on both countries to coordinate, but it would be premature to describe them as a unified military bloc. The larger point is that coercive pressure has not isolated Tehran as completely as Washington might have hoped. It has also given US rivals opportunities to exploit the gaps in sanctions enforcement and the costs of a prolonged confrontation.Check on imperial presidencyThe Democratic victory in the midterms was sweeping. The party captured both the House of Representatives and the Senate, making gains in states and constituencies that had long been difficult terrain. Republicans lost ground in places including Kansas, South Carolina and Texas, while Democrats made inroads across the Rust Belt and Great Plains.Control of Congress gives Democrats more than a platform to criticise Trump. Committee gavels bring subpoena power, investigative hearings and the ability to demand documents and testimony from administration officials. Congressional committees can examine the intelligence behind the Iran operation, the legal basis for the strikes, the administration's assessment of the risks to shipping and energy supplies, and the arrangements made with Venezuela over oil and political transition.The War Powers Resolution of 1973 is another potential instrument. Democrats can use it to force votes on the continuation of hostilities and challenge the president's authority to sustain military operations without congressional approval. Congress can also use its control over funding and authorisations to put pressure on the administration, although any binding legislative measure could face a presidential veto.The result is a president who remains commander-in-chief but now faces a more hostile legislature, greater scrutiny and a potentially difficult fight over the resources required to continue the conflict. The midterms have not ended the Iran war, but they have made its domestic political management considerably harder.The irony was not lost even on Trump. After the Democratic sweep, he acknowledged that "a part of it was Iran". But he stood by the decision, telling The Wall Street Journal: "I did the right thing. I would have done it again."The Islamic Republic of Iran has survived its supreme leader's death, with power passing to his son and the security establishment gaining influence. Meanwhile, the American president who projected strength overseas has been handed a powerful reality check in his own country.ALSO READ |'Trump hasn’t done anything to help': Republicans blame MAGA chief for midterm routYou use AI every day. articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Congress on Wednesday described the Centre's decision to extend Agniveers' service tenure by two years as a "U-turn", claiming it was driven by the upcoming assembly elections in Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Uttarakhand, where many young people aspire to join the armed forces."Elections are approaching in Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, and Uttarakhand. A large number of youth from these states want to join the armed forces. So, they (government) took a U-turn out of fear," Congress MP Pawan Khera told ANI.Also Read | Good news for Agniveers: Government extends tenure by two yearsOf the three states, the BJP, which leads the government at the Centre, will seek a third consecutive term in Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand.Reacting to the announcement by Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) General NS Raja Subramani, Khera said the Congress had opposed the Agnipath scheme from the beginning as it would "adversely affect" the armed forces and the future of young recruits."We had opposed the Agniveer scheme right from the beginning. (LoP) Rahul Gandhi ji opposed it too. This scheme is harming not just our armed forces but also the youth of the country — you would leave them unemployed on the streets after another two years," he added.Questioning the Centre's revised arrangement, under which 25% of Agniveers would be absorbed into the regular forces based on merit while the remaining 75% would receive a two-year extension, the Congress MP asked what would happen to those who were not selected after the extended tenure."They say they'll absorb 25% into the army and give the rest a two-year extension. You'll absorb 25%. What will happen to the other 75%? After two years, will they be out on the streets again, or will you take another U-turn?" he asked.Earlier on Wednesday, CDS General Subramani announced that Agniveers who were previously required to leave after completing their four-year tenure would be offered an additional two-year engagement period. Those willing to join the armed forces would subsequently be enrolled based on objective selection criteria.The Agnipath scheme was introduced by the Union Cabinet in June 2022 for recruitment into the armed forces for a four-year tenure. Under the original arrangement, one-fourth of Agniveers were eligible for enrolment in the regular forces based on merit, while the remaining three-fourths would return to civilian life after completing their service.The revision announcement comes amid criticism of the scheme over the short duration of service and the employment prospects of recruits after leaving the armed forces.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: French blood plasma storage hit by hackers in widening cyberattack campaign
articles.summary: A cyberattack targeting refrigeration systems at three French blood bank sites attempted to raise storage temperatures to extremely high levels, but was
articles.body: A cyberattack targeting refrigeration systems at three French blood bank sites attempted to raise storage temperatures to extremely high levels, but was detected and thwarted before any blood products or samples were compromised, French authorities said.The incident on Monday targeted a supplier of refrigeration equipment used by the French Blood Establishment (EFS), which oversees the country's blood collection and distribution network.The attack accompanies a wider wave of cyberattacks on refrigeration systems across Europe, with supermarkets in several countries reporting spoiled food after hackers remotely tampered with their fridges and freezers, causing losses worth millions of euros.The EFS said in a statement late Tuesday that temperature and defrosting thresholds at three of its plasma storage sites had been raised to extremely high levels. However, monitoring and alarm systems quickly detected the irregularities, allowing staff to intervene before any damage was caused.“No health consequences have been identified, and no blood products were lost,” the EFS said.In a statement to Sky News, the EFS said the incident had affected a limited number of its sites and that further technical information from its service provider would help establish its full extent.It said monitoring and alarm systems had rapidly detected the changes in the cold-room systems, allowing staff to protect stored blood products and samples.The EFS said it could not yet comment on the origin of the incident or identify those responsible, adding that all products and samples in the affected equipment had been secured or transferred as a precaution.The affected facilities stored plasma bags intended for transfusions as well as plasma used in the manufacture of medicines. All products and samples were either secured or transferred to other facilities as a precaution, it said.The EFS said its blood collection and distribution operations remained uninterrupted, ensuring continued supplies to hospitals and healthcare facilities. It has also stepped up monitoring of refrigeration equipment across its network.France's national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, and the health ministry are investigating the incident.You use AI every day. articles.title: An Oregon couple turned part of their one-acre lawn into a vegetable garden; it has now helped deliver 10 tons of free food to families in need
articles.summary: When Jean-Marie and Cory Buxton bought a one-acre property in Corvallis, Oregon, in 2018, they saw an opportunity to do more with the land than simply
articles.body: When Jean-Marie and Cory Buxton bought a one-acre property in Corvallis, Oregon, in 2018, they saw an opportunity to do more with the land than simply maintain a lawn. The couple removed a portion of the grass, planted organic vegetables and created a fruit orchard, turning their backyard into a food-growing initiative for people facing food insecurity. What started as a family effort has since expanded into a network involving local farmers, backyard gardeners, private donors and Oregon State University. Through their initiative, called The Farmette Project, the Buxtons have helped distribute 10 tons of free fresh produce to food banks, free food stands and Native American communities by the 2025 growing season.How an Oregon couple turned their lawn into a food-producing gardenThe idea took shape when the Buxtons moved to Oregon's Willamette Valley and noticed the contrast between the region's agricultural abundance and the limited access to fresh produce in some nearby communities. While the valley produced plenty of fruits and vegetables, some communities along the Oregon coast faced difficulties accessing fresh food because of their local growing conditions.Jean-Marie, who had previously worked in social services and volunteered on a Native American reservation in South Dakota, was particularly interested in improving access to nutritious food. During her earlier volunteering, she had seen families receive food supplies that lacked the freshness and quality she believed they deserved.The couple decided to put their available land to use. They removed around one-third of their lawn to grow organic crops and dedicated another third to a fruit orchard. Their sons and a friend helped prepare the soil, spread compost and turn the grassy property into a productive growing space.Jean-Marie named the initiative The Farmette Project, with the aim of growing and distributing fresh food to people who needed it.The backyard garden grew into a wider food networkThe project initially focused on growing vegetables on the family's property. During its first growing season, the garden produced around 1,700 pounds of tomatoes, providing more than enough for the intended recipients and several local food banks.However, the Buxtons soon realised that they could collect food from other sources rather than depend entirely on their own harvest. Jean-Marie approached private donors, commercial farms and Oregon State University to ask for surplus fruits and vegetables.The network gradually expanded as local growers and residents began contributing. An Oregon State University professor allowed the project to collect tomatoes from the outside rows of a university research plot. Other residents offered fruit from their gardens, including figs and blueberries.Local volunteers also joined the effort, helping harvest and collect produce that might otherwise have gone unused. The project now brings together different growers and donors across the Willamette Valley, creating a supply of fresh food that extends well beyond the family's original garden.How the project delivered 10 tons of free fresh produceBy the 2025 growing season, The Farmette Project had reached its goal of delivering 10 tons of free fresh produce. That is equivalent to approximately 20,000 pounds of fruits and vegetables.The food is distributed through local food banks, free food stands and partner organisations serving Native American communities. The Buxtons coordinate deliveries during the summer harvest, with the distribution season lasting around 12 weeks.Their work also involves transporting produce from different growing locations to distribution centres. Cory shares responsibility for growing, harvesting and collecting fruits and vegetables from across the Willamette Valley, including taking supplies to a partner distribution centre on the Oregon coast.The initiative has also helped connect growers who have more produce than they can use with communities that have limited access to fresh fruits and vegetables. Some of the receiving communities have even introduced canning classes to help residents preserve the seasonal harvest for later use.How Jean-Marie finances the initiative through handmade soapsThe Farmette Project operates largely through the couple's volunteer efforts and self-funding. Neither Jean-Marie nor Cory takes a salary for their work on the initiative, according to their account to Points of Light.Jean-Marie uses her experience as a soap maker, developed over around 25 years, to sell handmade soaps and crafts. The money helps cover the project's expenses and allows her to purchase additional produce, including items such as melons and berries, at discounted prices.The project also works with farmers who offer matching arrangements, allowing money spent on produce to go further. In some cases, every dollar contributed towards purchasing food is matched by participating growers.During the peak summer season, the initiative can demand as much as 160 hours of work each month. This includes coordinating with growers, organising volunteers, collecting produce and arranging deliveries.The couple wants to continue the projectReaching the 10-ton milestone has not marked the end of the Buxtons' work. They intend to continue distributing fresh produce and strengthen relationships with the communities and organisations they serve.For Jean-Marie, one of the most meaningful aspects has been building relationships with Native American communities and ensuring that families and elders have access to fresh food. She has also emphasised the importance of respecting recipients' privacy and dignity rather than making the assistance about the people delivering it.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
